 Democrats won control of Congress. Their economic agenda is set to target healthcare, tariffs, and Trump's allies. 
 Live Midterms 2026 election results and latest updates: Mississippi votes still being counted in Senate nail-biter after Democrats take control of Congress
 As Democrats took a victory lap, President Trump distanced himself from a dismal GOP showing as the White House was left to reckon with a historic rout.
 Yahoo News Staff Updated Thu, November 5, 2026 at 10:12 PM UTC Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Supporters of James Talarico react during a midterm election night watch party in Austin. (Brandon Bell via Getty Images) Democrats continue to celebrate one of the most lopsided midterm election victories in modern U.S. history, routing their Republican rivals to gain control of the U.S. House, U.S. Senate and statehouses across the country.
 In the Senate, Democrats flipped seven seats and now hold 54 to the Republican Party's 44. Two seats — nail-biting contests in Alaska and Mississippi — remain undeclared.
 To do so, Democrats won a series of key battleground contests. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers in one of the most closely watched races of the midterms. James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, becoming the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in the Lone Star State since 1988.  Annie Andrews beat Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina to flip a Senate seat. In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson defeated incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, putting an end to her three-decade tenure. Sen. Jon Ossoff comfortably won reelection in Georgia. Other Senate seats to flip to the Democratic Party included Roy Cooper in North Carolina, Sherrod Brown in Ohio, Josh Turek in Iowa and Adam Hamilton in Kansas.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement In the House, Democrats held 251 House seats to the GOP's 155 as of 3 p.m. ET Thursday, comfortably passing the majority threshold of 218, with 29 races still to be called. The latest estimates show that the party is on track to win its largest majority since 2008. And there are still seats it could flip, including Colorado's Fourth District, which is held by Republican incumbent Rep. Lauren Boebert, a staunch Trump ally, whose race against Democrat Eileen Laubacher remains tight.
 There were also 36 gubernatorial races , mayoral contests and numerous ballot measures — and plenty of firsts. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia became the first Black woman elected governor in U.S. history, while Democrat Amy Acton became the first woman elected governor of Ohio. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds became the state's first Black governor-elect. El-Sayed will be America's first Muslim senator.
 At the White House, President Trump signaled he would work with Democrats during his remaining two years in office but said he wouldn't hesitate to use his veto power. The president also acknowledged Wednesday that the Iran war contributed to Republican losses, but defended his decision to pursue the conflict. "If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," he said, adding: "You can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon."
 Vice President JD Vance had earlier blamed the scale of GOP losses on the war with Iran.
 "The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," he wrote in a post on X . "The reason we lost is the war."
 Live 184 updates Featured Thu, Nov 05, 2026 07:57 PM UTC Kate Murphy Democrat Nithya Raman wins Los Angeles mayor's race, defeating incumbent Karen Bass
 Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman speaks at an election night event on Tuesday.
 (AP Photo/Jae C. Hong) Nithya Raman, a democratic socialist, has defeated embattled incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayor's race, according to the Associated Press. Bass's single term was marked by the fallout from the deadly Palisades and Eaton Fires in 2025.
 Bass conceded to Raman on Thursday, writing in a statement that serving as the mayor of L.A. "has been the honor of my life."
 "Four years ago, you elected me as the first Black woman mayor in the history of Los Angeles," Bass said. "You gave me the honor of serving the city that raised me, and every single day since, I have carried that responsibility with me."
 Raman's campaign focused on addressing homelessness, housing costs and change at City Hall.
 The city council member defeated Spencer Pratt, a Republican and former reality TV personality, in June's nonpartisan primary.
 Raman, the first Indian American to lead Los Angeles, will also prepare the city to host the 2028 Olympics.
 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 10:06 PM UTC Mike Bebernes Democratic senator: Some of our 'sacrificial lambs' were shocked to find out they actually won
 Democrat Ruben Gallego of Arizona told reporters on Thursday that some of the candidates his party put on the state's ballot to effectively serve as placeholders ended up winning races they never imagined they could win. 
 "We won in districts that we didn't know existed," he said. "We actually had to call up some of our friends that put up sacrificial lambs and tell them that they won."
 "One of them remarked, 'What are you talking about? That was not the plan,'" he added.
 Though some races are still undecided, Arizona Democrats appear to be on track to hold majorities in both chambers of the state legislature for the first time in 60 years.
 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 09:09 PM UTC Kate Murphy Pete Aguilar announces bid for House majority whip
 Rep. Pete Aguilar speaks at a news conference in Washington on Wednesday.
 (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite) House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar announced on Thursday in a letter to colleagues that he's throwing his hat in the ring for House majority whip.
 "With a Democratic majority, we'll have the tools to rein in this out-of-control administration and investigate the agencies, officials and corporations that have been making life harder and more expensive for our communities," the California Democrat wrote. "I look forward to working with each of you to deliver on our affordability agenda."
 House majority whip is the third-highest ranking position in the party's House leadership, behind the House speaker and the majority leader.
 House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York announced his candidacy for speaker, while Katherine Clark of Massachusetts announced her bid for majority leader.
 Aguilar, Jeffries and Clark have no challengers at the moment.
 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 08:43 PM UTC Dylan Stableford Schumer says Democrats will not let Trump put a 'right-winger' on the Supreme Court
 Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer speaks in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 4.
 (AP Photo/Allison Robbert) With Democrats soon to have clear majorities in the House and Senate, Sen. Chuck Schumer, the leader of the chamber's Democratic caucus, said on Thursday that the party will not allow President Trump to put "a right-winger" on the Supreme Court once it assumes power.
 In an interview with the Associated Press , Schumer — who is expected to again become Senate majority leader next year — would not say if he would hold a Supreme Court vacancy open until the next presidential election like former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell did in 2016. (If there's a vacancy before Democrats formally take control of the Senate in January, Trump could nominate — and the GOP could confirm — a replacement while Republicans still have a majority.)
 But Schumer did say that Democrats are "not going to allow any crappy nominees" to be confirmed to the nation's highest court while Trump is in office.
 "The bottom line is we're not going to allow a right-winger on the court," Schumer said.
 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 08:24 PM UTC Kate Murphy Democrats have won 251 seats in the U.S. House, the most since 2008
 Democrats have officially won 251 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives, according to the Associated Press . It's well beyond the 218 needed to secure a majority in the chamber, and final votes are still being counted.
 It's part of the massive blue wave from Tuesday's midterm elections, with Democrats so far flipping 41 seats.
 The majority is the largest in the House since the 2008 election, when Democrats won 257 seats.

 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 07:03 PM UTC Kate Murphy Democrat Scott Colom widens lead over GOP incumbent in Mississippi Senate race
 The Mississippi Senate race remains a nail-biter and too close to call. On Thursday afternoon, Democratic candidate Scott Colom expanded his narrow lead over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
 Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by 1,724 votes as of 12:45 p.m. ET, according to the Associated Press .
 Colom has 49% of the vote, while Hyde-Smith has 48.9% of the vote. So far, 96% of the votes have been counted.
 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 03:52 PM UTC Kate Murphy Trump says votes for 2nd 'Dan Sullivan' should go to GOP incumbent as Alaska Senate race remains uncalled
 Dan S. Sullivan and Dan J. Sullivan.
 (Photo illustration: Yahoo News; photos: Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images, Katie Holmlund/AP) Alaska's Senate race remains uncalled as of Thursday morning as the state continues to count mail-in ballots. Democrat Mary Peltola currently leads incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by 637 votes, according to the Associated Press .
 Alaska uses ranked choice voting , which means the state's elections require a candidate to earn a majority of votes to win. If no candidate has a majority of voter support, the last-ranked candidate is eliminated and Alaska is allowed to hold an instant runoff, which would take place on Nov. 18 in this case.
 Voters who ranked the eliminated candidate first have their vote counted for their second choice. This continues until one candidate receives the majority of the vote.
 President Trump on Thursday said Sullivan would "easily" win the Alaska Senate race if he were given the votes from the other candidate on the ballot with nearly the same name, Daniel J. Sullivan, a former teacher.
 "The vote totals for the Fake Dan Sullivan, plus the other 'slug' that the Dems put on the Ballot, should be immediately given to the REAL Dan Sullivan, and the Election is over - He easily wins. There is no other fair solution!" Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social .
 The Justice Department has accused Peltola's campaign of ballot stacking to potentially confuse voters and siphon away votes from the Republican incumbent.
 Peltola has denied being aware of the alleged scheme. "I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about," Peltola said during an October campaign rally.
 Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have also repeatedly denied involvement in any campaign scheme. Dan J. Sullivan has also long denied he was recruited to participate in the alleged scheme.
 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 03:05 PM UTC Kate Murphy A 19-year-old ASU student is set to become the next Maricopa County clerk of the Superior Court
 A 19-year-old sophomore at Arizona State University is set to become the next Maricopa County clerk of the Superior Court in Arizona.
 Sebastian Matta, a Democrat, has taken the lead in the race against Republican opponent Jeff Dial.
 Maricopa County results as of Wednesday evening showed Matta in the lead with 53.4% of the vote, while Dial had 46.6% of the vote.
 The office manages official court records and financial services for the justice system in the nation's fourth-largest county.
 The race has not been officially called, but ABC15 Arizona reported that Dial called Matta to concede.
 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 01:50 PM UTC Harriet Sinclair Trump backs Hegseth as questions remain over his role
 Questions are swirling around whether President Trump will retain Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth following the GOP's defeat at the midterms, much of which has been attributed to the ongoing Iran war.
 Multiple sources told CBS that Trump had asked advisers whether to replace the defense secretary — as George W. Bush did with Donald Rumsfeld following the 2006 midterms — however, other sources told the news outlet no decision has been made as yet.
 Trump himself said he is not planning to replace Hegseth. Asked on Wednesday whether he would replace Hegseth, Trump told reporters : "No, I think he's doing a very good job."

 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 01:06 PM UTC Stuart Henderson The numbers that show the scale of Democrats' midterm rout
 Midterms tend to be backlash elections, and the sitting president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his performance in office.
 This year, Democrats comprehensively routed their Republican rivals , regaining control of the U.S. House, U.S. Senate and statehouses across the country. Along the way, they shattered a series of decades-long Republican winning streaks and notched several historic firsts .
 In the House, Democrats could end up flipping 40+ seats once the count is fully completed. That could lead to a majority of about 255, the largest since 2008, and possibly since 1992.
 Democrats have already flipped seven seats in the Senate, and that could reach nine once Alaska and Mississippi are called. That hasn't happened for either party since 2014. The last time a party flipped more than nine Senate seats in a midterm election was 1958.
 Read Yahoo's Andrew Romano's deep dive into the numbers for more insights. 
 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 12:38 PM UTC Harriet Sinclair Why is the Mississippi race so close?
 The nail-biter Senate race in Mississippi remains too close to call in this historically red state.
 Democratic candidate Scott Colom has 49% of the vote, while Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith has 48.9% of the vote — just 1,138 votes separate the two out of more than 948,000 cast so far.
 County clerks have 10 days to certify the election.
 If Colom wins, he will become the first Democratic candidate to be elected to the Senate from Mississippi since 1982, and the first Black US senator elected in the state since 1875.
 The potential flip mirrors the blue wave that has swept the midterms, which many see as a reflection of the Trump administration and the president's low approval ratings, propelled by issues including the Iran war and rising prices.
 But in Mississippi, there are other factors at play. Aaron Hitefield, an assistant professor of political science at Mississippi State University, told Time magazine that Hyde-Smith's campaign lacked luster.
 Hyde-Smith won reelection in 2020 by 10 points compared with Mississippi's other Republican Senator, Roger Wicker, who scored a 25-point lead in his 2024 win.
 She did not "do the groundwork necessary to run a successful campaign," Hitefield said, adding: "Even if she does win, she didn't do, really, what she needed to win with any sort of safety. "
 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 12:01 PM UTC Harriet Sinclair Which races are yet to be called?
 While Democrats have taken control of both the House and Senate, there are a number of races yet to be called that will determine the size of the Democrats' majority.
 Senate races 
 In the Senate, Democrats have 54 seats, while Republicans have 44, according to the latest figures from the Associated Press. Two races have yet to be called: Mississippi and Alaska.
 In Mississippi , Democratic candidate Scott Colom has 49% of the vote, while Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith has 48.9% of the vote — just 1,138 votes out of more than 948,000 that have already been counted separate the two. County clerks have 10 days to certify the election.
 In Alaska , Democratic candidate Mary Peltola has 48.2% of the vote, while Republican Dan Sullivan has 47.9%, according to AP. A number of votes come from rural areas, and the state, which runs a ranked-choice voting system, will accept ballots mailed from outside the U.S. (and postmarked by Election Day) until Nov. 18.
 House races 
 In the House, Democrats currently hold 240 seats while Republicans have 147. There are 48 yet to be called — including New York's 17th and Colorado's 4th districts.
 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 11:22 AM UTC Andrew Romano Midterms 2026: How Democrats built a blue wave and won control of Congress
 On Tuesday, the Democratic Party shattered a series of decades-long Republican winning streaks, notched several historic firsts and flipped both the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives.
 The results mean President Trump will no longer enjoy complete Republican control of Congress and, starting in January, Democrats in the House and Senate will have the power to block parts of the president's agenda, reject his nominees and investigate his administration.
 Read the full analysis from Yahoo's Andrew Romano.

 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 10:38 AM UTC Harriet Sinclair Sanders says Democrats are 'not very popular' despite midterms win
 Sen. Bernie Sanders has described the Democratic Party as "not very popular," despite the blue wave that dominated the midterm elections.
 Speaking on Wednesday in an interview with the BBC, Sanders, an Independent who caucuses with the Democrats, said: "What are the Democrats offering? I mean, you tell me, and I am a member of the caucus."
 He said Democrats now had to ensure they focus on the "crisis facing working people."
 Asked whether the Democrats were likely to "go after" President Trump and his family now they have control of Congress, Sanders replied: "Of course." He added that Trump must be "held accountable" for the Republicans' defeat.
 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 10:03 AM UTC Harriet Sinclair Boebert locked in knife-edge race in Colorado's Fourth District
 Rep. Lauren Boebert at an election night watch party in Windsor, Colo.
 (RJ Sangosti/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images via Getty Images) The race for Colorado's Fourth District remains uncalled — with incumbent Lauren Boebert attempting to hold on in what was widely considered the state's "safest" Republican seat.
 Boebert currently has 48% of the vote, while her Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher has 48.7%, according to the latest figures from the Associated Press.
 With 93% of the ballots cast, Boebert trails by 2,513 votes.
 Colorado's 4th congressional district last elected a Democrat in 2008.
 Thu, Nov 05, 2026 09:23 AM UTC Harriet Sinclair Senate race remains on knife-edge in Mississippi
 Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, left, and Democrat Scott Colom.
 (Photo illustration: Yahoo News, Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images, Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today via AP) The Senate race in Mississippi has turned into a nail-biter, with the contest still too close to call and 96% of the expected vote counted.
 According to the latest figures from the Associated Press, Democratic candidate Scott Colom has 49% of the vote, while Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith has 48.9% of the vote.
 The race is still uncalled because officials are waiting on two batches of ballots, with one of those containing affidavit ballots, largely filed by people who did not show up at the polls with voter ID or had been marked as inactive on voter rolls.
 The state has 10 days — in this case, until Nov. 13 — to certify the election.
 However, regardless of how close the count is, there is no automatic legal recourse for a vote count . Mississippi is the only state that doesn't have a law allowing for recounts of close statewide races, and candidates would need a court order to get a recount, which would likely happen after Nov. 13.
 Wed, Nov 04, 2026 11:38 PM UTC Mike Bebernes White House: Democrats' midterm wins aren't an 'obituary' for Trump's presidency
 The White House on Wednesday pledged to "defy the odds" in the wake of sweeping Democratic victories that saw Republicans lose control of both chambers of Congress. 
 "Every time the Radical Left, the Fake News, and the professional panic class have written President Trump's obituary, they have been wrong. They will be wrong again," the White House wrote in a press release. 
 Unified control of Congress gives Democrats the potential opportunity to pass legislation rolling back parts of Trump's agenda, but the president signaled Tuesday night that he plans to use his veto power to block them, if necessary. 
 "In the final two years of his presidency, Democrats will try — and fail — to reverse everything President Trump has done," the White House wrote Wednesday.

 Wed, Nov 04, 2026 11:20 PM UTC Andrew Romano When will we know the Senate result in Mississippi? 
 The Senate race between Democrat Scott Colom and incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi — one of the reddest states in America — wasn't supposed to be especially close.
 But now it couldn't be closer. As of Wednesday afternoon, Colom was leading by just 65 votes. The race is still uncalled, because officials are waiting on two remaining batches of ballots.
 District Attorney and U.S. Senate candidate for Mississippi Scott Colom.
 The first batch comes from 11 counties that have yet to report 10% or more of their returns. The other batch contains affidavit ballots, which were generally filed by people who did not show up at the polls with voter ID or had been marked as inactive on voter rolls. 
 So when will we know more — and what's likely to happen?
 County clerks in Mississippi have 10 days — in this case, until Nov. 13 — to certify the election.
 Five of the counties with outstanding ballots have favored Colom, including Hinds (the most populous in the state). Five have favored Hyde-Smith. One is a toss-up. Any mail ballots from those counties must arrive by Tuesday, Nov. 10, in order to count. 
 Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
 As for the affidavit ballots, voters need to validate them with ID by the same day: Nov. 10. The Colom campaign has said that roughly 10,000 to 15,000 affidavit ballots were filed this year.
 So we should know more by early next week.
 There's no recount procedure in Mississippi, but if the count is still super close at that point, Colom or Hyde-Smith could challenge certain ballots in court. That would likely happen after certification on Nov. 13.
 Wed, Nov 04, 2026 10:57 PM UTC Mike Bebernes Mississippi is the only state with no recount law
 Every state but Mississippi has a law on the books allowing for recounts of close statewide races, and Mississippi is the very state that may end up having the closest race of the 2026 midterms. 
 As of Wednesday afternoon, the Senate race between incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde‑Smith and Democrat Scott Colom had a margin of just 65 votes with 95% of ballots counted. But no matter how tight the final result is, there is no law providing for a recount.
 In 26 states, recounts are automatically triggered in races where the margin falls below a certain percentage of the vote, often set at 0.5%. In other states, the law allows the losing candidate to request a recount or provides a pathway for a legal challenge that can lead to one.
 The loser in Mississippi could try to challenge the result in court, potentially leading to a court-ordered recount or to the exclusion of certain ballots, but the law does not provide a direct path for that.
 Wed, Nov 04, 2026 10:21 PM UTC Mike Bebernes A look at the Senate map with 2 races still undecided
 The story of the Senate on Tuesday was Democrats defending all of their vulnerable seats while notching win after win in historically Republican territory. As of Wednesday afternoon, they had secured a net gain of at least seven seats — well clear of the four they needed to flip control of the chamber. 
 Only two races remain up in the air, both of which are currently held by Republicans. With vote tallies extremely close in both Alaska and Mississippi, it may be some time before we know exactly how big the Democrats' majority will be when the new Congress convenes in January.
